U3500.d: U3500 says that supply input A of a module is present but its voltage is implausible, for example outside the window expected for the current power mode or contradicting other measurements, without clearly passing a lower or upper limit. It thus sits between U3006, which reports a missing or open feed, and the hard limit codes U3501 and U3502.
s: Functions of the module dropping out or behaving inconsistently
Code returns mainly under electrical load
c: High-resistance terminal or fuse contact on feed A
Poor module ground shifting the measured supply
Drifting voltage measurement inside the module

U3501.d: U3501 reports that supply A of a module is below its permitted range. GM's electric brake booster (BSC2) in the 2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables runs two checks: the CAN/logic supply under 7.5 V for 0.09 s, and the internal sensor for the module supply under 4.9 V for 0.2 s, a level below the point where the hardware should already have shut down.
s: Module resets or drops off the network at low voltage
Other self-tests of the module suspended
Warning lamp for the affected system, usually without MIL
c: Deep voltage dip during engine start
Corroded fuse, terminal or ground in the A feed
Internal supply stage of the module faulty

U3502.d: U3502 means supply A rises above its allowed limit. In GM's 2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables the electric brake booster checks its CAN supply voltage and sets U3502 above 16 V lasting 0.09 s while its software runs; this is Type B, so the MIL comes on after two failing trips, and the test passes after 30 s with ignition on.
s: MIL after repeated trips
Several modules logging overvoltage at once
Flickering lights or battery warning
c: Generator regulator or DC/DC converter overcharging
Jump start or external charger with excessive voltage
Loose battery terminal causing voltage spikes
Faulty voltage measurement inside the module

U3503.d: U3503 stands for a supply A that keeps jumping: mostly correct, but with brief dropouts or spikes, so the module sees erratic readings or restarts. What sets it apart from U3501 and U3502 is the pattern rather than the level: short interruptions, fast swings between samples or repeated resets.
s: Sporadic resets or brief function dropouts
Code returns over bumps or when loads switch
c: Loose crimp, pin or fuse contact in feed A
Ground shared with heavy loads causing dips
Cracked solder joint inside the module

U3504.d: U3504 checks the plausibility of the second supply input, B. Modules with high-power stages often split their supply: in GM's electric brake booster tables B is the battery feed of the booster circuit (voltage sensor 1), checked separately against low and high limits and compared with feed C.
s: Power stage functions weak or switched off under load
Code mainly when motors or valves are active
c: Resistance in fuse, connector or ground of feed B under load
Feed B supplied from a different source than expected
Drifting measurement of feed B inside the module

U3505.d: U3505 reports that supply input B is too low. In GM's 2016–2019 hybrid tables the electric brake booster treats B as the battery feed of the booster circuit and checks it at several levels: sensor reading under 6 V for 30 s, battery voltage under 9.3 V for 90 s, and quick 0.2 s checks with reduced assist once it falls below 9.3 V (level 1) or 7.5 V (level 2); all Special Type C, no MIL.
s: Functions on the second feed missing, e.g. warm A/C
Reduced brake assist with warning on booster modules
Stored together with U3018
c: Fuse of feed B blown by a short elsewhere on the circuit
Corroded terminal or ground in feed B
Internal measurement or supply path faulty

U3506.d: U3506 reports overvoltage on supply input B. In GM's electric brake booster (2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables) three checks feed this code: battery voltage of the booster circuit above 17 V for 90 s, the supply of the internal motor driver above 18 V for 1.1 s, and battery voltage above 16.5 V for 1.1 s, at which booster performance is cut back.
s: MIL after two trips
Reduced assist of the supplied power stage
Overvoltage codes in further modules
c: Charging voltage too high from regulator or DC/DC converter
Jump starter or charger delivering excessive voltage
Faulty measurement of feed B in the module

U3507.d: U3507 covers an unsteady supply B: the voltage is mostly in range but drops out or jumps for short moments. Since B often powers stages such as motors or valves, the dropouts typically appear when these draw current, for instance while braking or steering.
s: Brief function dropouts when power stages switch on
Code returns sporadically and is hard to reproduce
c: Loose crimp or worn fuse holder in feed B
Corroded ground point of the module

U3508.d: U3508 checks the plausibility of a third supply input, C. Only modules with large or separately protected loads have three feeds; in GM's electric brake booster (2016–2019 hybrid tables) C is the motor driver feed, measured by voltage sensor 2 and compared with feed B through U3019 (ratio outside 0.766 to 1.321).
s: Reduced function of the motor-driven system
Correlation codes between feeds stored as well
c: Resistance in the motor supply path of feed C
Poor ground of the power stage
Drift of the internal voltage divider

U3509.d: U3509 says supply C is too low. In GM's 2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables the electric brake booster sets it when voltage sensor 2, which watches the motor driver supply, reads below 6 V for 90 s while the car travels faster than 4 mph.
s: MIL and brake warning on the first trip
Harder brake pedal through missing assist
c: Fuse of the motor supply open
Broken wire or failed connector in feed C
Internal measurement of feed C faulty

U350A.d: U350A is the overvoltage code for supply C. GM's electric brake booster (2016–2019 hybrid tables) logs it when voltage sensor 2 on the motor driver supply exceeds 19.8 V for 90 s at speeds above 4 mph, Type A, so a single failing trip lights the MIL.
s: MIL and brake warning on the first trip
Brake assist reduced or switched off
c: Generator regulator or DC/DC converter overcharging
Jump start from a 24 V source
Faulty measurement of feed C inside the module

U350B.d: U350B reports that supply C fluctuates: it drops or spikes briefly without staying out of range. Where C feeds a motor stage, as in GM's electric brake booster (motor driver supply, voltage sensor 2), such faults surface at moments of peak current, because a loose contact then loses voltage or opens for an instant.
s: Brief loss of assist from the motor-driven function
Sporadic warning lamp that clears again
c: Loose fuse contact or ring terminal in feed C or its ground

U350C.d: U350C reports that the fan built into or attached to a control module draws no current, or its circuit is open, at the moment the module switches it on. Some electronics carry their own blower: on the 2021 Toyota RAV4 Prime the plug-in charger has a fan with a speed sensor (bulletin T-SB-0021-21, code P1CE931), and the central infotainment unit of the Karma Revero has one under a shroud (TB-24-94-01).
s: Module fan silent when it should run
Module overheats, reduces output, charges slower or restarts
Temperature warning or function message for the affected module
c: Fan motor winding or brushes open
Fan plug loose or not latched after the module was removed
Broken fan supply or control wire
Fan output stage inside the module failed open

U350D.d: U350D is set when the voltage or current feedback in a control module's fan circuit sits below the window the module expects. Usually the fan supply or control wire touches ground, or the motor itself has shorted turns, so the output stage limits current or switches off and the fan stands still; a blown fan fuse produces the same picture.
s: Module fan does not run
Reduced function or shutdown of the module when hot
Blown fan fuse
c: Fan supply or control wire chafed through to ground
Fan motor with shorted windings drawing excess current
Fan fuse blown as a result of the short
Output stage in the module pulling the line low

U350E.d: U350E points to a fan circuit whose level is higher than the module expects, typically because the control or feedback line is shorted to battery voltage or the output stage is stuck on. Unlike the low and open faults, the fan may then run all the time, even with the module cold or the car parked, which is audible and can drain the 12 V battery.
s: Module fan running continuously, also after switch-off
12 V battery discharged after standing
Fan does not react to temperature changes
c: Fan control or feedback wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Fan output stage in the module stuck on
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the fan connector

U350F.d: U350F means the fan circuit is electrically sound but the fan does not do what it is told: its speed feedback disagrees with the command, or the module keeps heating up although the fan is switched on. Dust, a blocked or rubbing blade, worn bearings or a lost speed signal are typical.
s: Fan noise, rattling or whining from the module
Module runs hot, charging or function slowed
Code returns after clearing once the fan is commanded again
c: Fan blade blocked by dust, debris or a deformed shroud
Worn fan bearing slowing the fan down
Fan speed sensor signal missing or misread
Module software misjudging the fan feedback (Toyota RAV4 Prime charger)

U3510.d: U3510 says a control module lacks a calibration it needs: either the data set that adapts its software to the vehicle was never written or got lost, or a learned calibration such as a sensor alignment has not been done. CARB makes every emission-critical unit report a calibration ID and a verification number, so empty or invalid data cannot pass unnoticed.
s: Function of the affected module unavailable or limited
Warning lamp of the related system, MIL if the module is OBD-relevant
Fault appears right after a module replacement or software update
c: New or used module installed without programming or setup
Software update aborted, e.g. by low 12 V voltage or lost connection
Required learn or alignment routine not performed after repair
Internal memory of the module losing its stored data

U3511.d: U3511 is the general fault of a second high-voltage interlock loop, circuit B. Many vehicles need more than one loop: a Volvo truck patent gives each separate HV bus its own interlock circuit, and a Samsung SDI patent describes extra loops for battery-internal parts such as the service disconnect or the junction box, each with its own source, detector and diagnosis.
s: Vehicle does not enter ready mode
High-voltage or hybrid system warning in the cluster
Charging refused
c: HV connector, cover or disconnect in loop B open or not latched after service
Bent, pushed-back or corroded interlock pins
Interlock wiring of loop B chafed or cut
Source or sense stage for loop B in the monitoring module faulty

U3512.d: U3512 is stored when interlock loop B still conducts but behaves implausibly: its resistance drifts outside the permitted window, the returned signal does not follow the test pattern in time, or two readings of the same loop disagree. CATL's interlock patent explains why loops misreport: contact impedance between HV parts, supply fluctuations and static discharge can cause false alarms.
s: HV system switches off and on again unexpectedly
Ready mode lost while driving or at start
Interlock codes in several modules at once
c: Oxidised interlock pins raising the loop resistance
Connector in loop B seated but not fully latched
Harness rubbing on the body with intermittent contact
Interference or supply ripple distorting the loop signal

U3513.d: U3513 reports a signal on interlock loop B that stays below its lower limit while the loop is energised by the module. What that means depends on the circuit: where the module feeds a test voltage in and reads it back at the far end, an opened plug reads low just like a wire touching ground.
s: No ready mode, HV contactors stay open
Hybrid or EV warning lamp, MIL depending on maker
Charging not possible
c: Interlock wire of loop B chafed through to ground
Plug or cover in loop B open, read as low by the sensing circuit
Interlock source in the monitoring module not delivering its signal

U3514.d: U3514 means loop B reads higher than allowed: a wire of the loop touches 12 V or another supply, or the loop does not fall back to its low state once the module turns its source off. GM's loop A code checks both states, allowing 24 % of 5 V while the source is off and 44 % while it is on.
s: Vehicle will not start or enter ready mode
Service or HV warning lamp on
Fault stays present with all HV connectors properly mated
c: Interlock wire of loop B shorted to 12 V or another supply
Interlock source in the module not switching off
Water in a connector bridging an interlock pin to a supply pin
Incorrect splice or add-on wiring after a repair

U3515.d: U3515 is the general fault of a third interlock loop, circuit C. Such a loop exists where one or two are not enough: Caterpillar's patent for battery machines forms a separate interlock circuit from each battery group with its disconnect and contactor pair, and Samsung SDI mentions designs with more than two independent loops for parts inside the pack.
s: No ready mode, HV system switched off
Interlock codes for more than one loop stored together
Charging blocked
c: Connector or cover belonging to loop C opened during work and not refitted correctly
Interlock harness of loop C damaged
Fault in a coupled loop opening loop C as well
Monitoring module unable to drive or read loop C

U3516.d: U3516 flags loop C as electrically present but untrustworthy: resistance, timing or pattern of the returned signal fall outside what the module accepts, often only for moments. As the U35xx series has no intermittent code for loops B and C, unlike P0A0E for loop A, short dropouts will probably be stored here.
s: Sporadic loss of ready mode
HV warning that appears and clears by itself
Fault hard to reproduce in the workshop
c: Loose or spread contact in a connector of loop C
Twisted or strained harness section moving with the body
Static discharge or interference on the interlock line

U3517.d: U3517 says the level read back on interlock loop C stays too low. Depending on the design, an opened plug in loop C, a wire chafed to ground or a failed source in the monitoring module all lead to it.
s: Vehicle cannot be started
HV system warning in the instrument cluster
Charging unavailable
c: Interlock wire of loop C chafed to ground at a module or the body
Connector in loop C unplugged, sensed as a low signal
Broken interlock connector housing or terminal
Source stage for loop C failed in the monitoring module

U3518.d: U3518 is stored when loop C reads above its upper limit, usually a loop wire shorted to 12 V, to the wire of another loop in a shared connector, or a source stage that no longer switches off. Volvo's two-loop patent couples loops only through a galvanically isolated relay, so foreign voltage from one loop is not meant to reach another; where wires of different loops share a connector, damage can still bridge them.
s: No ready mode despite all HV connectors being in place
Service or HV warning lamp lit
High codes for more than one interlock loop
c: Interlock wire of loop C shorted to 12 V
Loop C bridged to another loop's wire in a shared connector
Interlock source for loop C stuck on in the module

U3519.d: U3519 marks a fault on the fourth interlock loop of the high-voltage system, circuit D, that the module does not classify further. A fourth independent loop mainly makes sense where one vehicle carries several battery packs.
s: One battery pack or high-voltage branch not available
Reduced range or power, or no ready mode at all, depending on design
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
c: Disconnect of the battery group on loop D left open or not locked after charging or service
Connector in loop D not fully latched
Loop D wiring damaged between packs or distribution units
Controller that drives and reads loop D faulty

U351A.d: U351A says that loop D returns a signal, but not the one the module sent out. Many designs feed the loop with pulses rather than a steady level.
s: Sudden loss of high-voltage power while driving or charging
Fault appears after rain, washing or on rough roads
Restart sometimes possible after switching off and on
c: Corroded or worn interlock contacts adding resistance to loop D
Moisture in a low-voltage connector of the loop
Loop wiring routed too close to switching high-voltage cables
Signal input of the evaluating controller faulty

U351B.d: U351B reports that too little level comes back from interlock loop D while the module drives it. GM's hybrid tables for the loop A code P0A0C give a frame of reference: the test only runs when on-board voltage exceeds 10.2 V, judges what fraction of a 5 V test signal returns against a 30 % limit and logs a Type A fault after two failed 12.5 ms readings.
s: No ready mode or high-voltage branch D unavailable
Warning to have the high-voltage system checked
Fault stays present after clearing until the wiring is repaired
c: Loop D wire pinched against the body and shorted to ground
Plug within loop D not seated after a repair
Test voltage source in the controller failed

U351C.d: U351C is stored when loop D carries more voltage than its present state allows. GM's high check for loop A, P0A0D, shows why both states are tested: with the source commanded to 0 V, more than 24 % of 5 V counts as a failure, five times in eight samples; with the source at 5 V the limit is 44 %, four times in six.
s: Vehicle does not reach ready mode
Fault returns immediately after clearing
Other 12 V consumers may show faults if a supply wire is involved
c: Loop D wire in contact with a 12 V supply line
Source driver in the controller no longer switches off
Earlier repair splice joined the loop to a wrong wire

U351D.d: U351D covers a disturbed fifth interlock loop, circuit E, where the module cannot narrow the fault down. Five loops arise naturally if every protected housing gets its own circuit.
s: No ready mode after work on a high-voltage component
High-voltage warning in the instrument cluster
c: Cover of a high-voltage housing on loop E not fitted or not fully tightened
Interlock contact or bridge in the cover bent or broken
Loop E wiring damaged between housings

U351E.d: U351E points to loop E giving results the module cannot trust, and the doubt may concern the monitoring hardware as much as the wiring. Designers do test their own test circuits: CATL first checks its current-generating stage so that a failing source is not blamed on high-voltage parts, and Sanden's interlock at the plug of an electric A/C compressor also recognises defects of the monitoring device and its loop, not
s: High-voltage shutdowns without a recognisable pattern
Fault returns although wiring and connectors test good
Possibly further self-test codes in the same controller
c: Current or voltage source for loop E drifting in the controller
Loose contact in a loop E connector
Detection circuit or its reference faulty
Controller software with outdated plausibility limits

U351F.d: U351F reports a low reading on interlock loop E, the usual result when a plug in that loop is separated or one of its wires is grounded. The US standard FMVSS 305a explains the hurry: a high-voltage connector that can be pulled without tools may, as one permitted option, bring its live parts to 60 V DC or less within one second of separation.
s: Abrupt loss of drive power, often with a stop-safely message
Vehicle cannot be restarted in ready mode
Charging aborted or impossible
c: High-voltage plug with interlock in loop E pulled or backed out
Loop E wire chafed through to ground
Interlock pin pushed back in its housing

U3520.d: U3520 means the fifth interlock loop sits above its permitted range, usually because a loop wire has picked up battery voltage or another low-voltage feed. Lear's patent for a pulsed interlock tester shows how to pin this down further: it measures current at generator and detector pins and, by comparing them, works out at which end the unwanted link to the 12 V side lies.
s: No ready mode, high-voltage warning shown
Fault reappears directly after clearing
c: Loop E wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Water or corrosion bridging a loop pin to a supply pin
Loop source in the controller stuck on

U3521.d: U3521 flags an unspecified fault in loop F, the sixth interlock loop. Extra loops often guard service openings rather than cables.
s: No ready mode after battery or service work
High-voltage system message in the cluster
c: Service disconnect not fully inserted or its lever not locked
Cover with interlock magnet missing, swapped or mounted out of position
Reed relay or switch contact of the cover interlock failed

U3522.d: U3522 is set when loop F behaves inconsistently, for instance when redundant evaluation channels reach different verdicts or the signal timing is off. Such checks exist because the interlock belongs to a safety function: Samsung SDI notes that it then needs an ASIL rating and failure-rate figures for its parts, so hidden faults in the monitoring path have to be caught, not just an open loop.
s: Ready mode occasionally refused, then available again
High-voltage warning that comes and goes
c: Redundant measuring channels for loop F disagree because of a sensing fault
Intermittent contact in a loop F connector
Internal fault of the evaluating controller

U3523.d: U3523 is logged when loop F reads too low, typically from an open plug or a wire shorted to ground. Tracing it means working close to high-voltage parts.
s: Vehicle not ready to drive, high-voltage warning shown
Charging not possible
c: Plug in loop F open or not engaged after service
Loop F wire shorted to ground
Broken interlock connector housing or locking tab

U3524.d: U3524 indicates a level on loop F above its upper threshold. Pulsed test schemes recognise this easily: if the loop is driven with a fixed square wave, as in Corun's 100 Hz battery design, a wire stuck at 12 V returns a flat level without any edges, which no intact connection could produce.
s: High-voltage system remains off, vehicle not ready
Code returns at once after clearing
c: Loop F wire chafed against a fused 12 V wire
Loop pin bridged to a neighbouring supply pin by corrosion or a bent terminal
Source driver for loop F no longer switches off

U3525.d: U3525 stands for a fault on the seventh interlock loop, circuit G, that the module does not classify further. Auxiliary high-voltage consumers are candidates for loops of their own: Sanden runs an interlock loop beside the HV plug between an electric A/C compressor and the traction battery, and a Chinese design cited by Caterpillar links an air-conditioning interlock circuit to the main one over CAN.
s: Air conditioning or electric heater unavailable
In some designs no ready mode at all
High-voltage or climate warning in the cluster
c: HV plug of an auxiliary consumer such as compressor or heater not latched
Loop G wiring to the auxiliary consumer damaged
Interlock contacts inside the consumer's connector damaged

U3526.d: U3526 reports an implausible result for loop G. Not every interlock is a wire loop: Rivian patented a virtual interlock in which a controller first brings the DC bus up to a low, safe voltage only, gathers the voltages that the high-voltage components report over CAN, and raises the bus to operating voltage only if those reports are acceptable.
s: Start-up of the high-voltage system aborted
Communication codes in other control units at the same time
c: Voltage sensing inside one high-voltage component faulty
Voltage message missing or late on the CAN bus
HV plug not fully seated, so one component sees no bus voltage

U3527.d: U3527 sets when the level on loop G drops below what the module expects. When several controllers watch interlock lines, the reporting unit already narrows the search.
s: Vehicle does not become ready, or charging is refused
Interlock codes in more than one control unit
c: Loop G wire cut or chafed to ground near a control unit
Plug in the section of the reporting unit not connected
Loop source of the reporting controller failed

U3528.d: U3528 means something lifts loop G to a level the controller never expects from it. Texas Instruments notes that automotive interlocks, unlike industrial ones, must survive a short to the 12 V battery and to ground; its reference design feeds the loop through an intelligent switch on the supply side with current limiting and thermal shutdown.
s: No ready mode, high-voltage warning
Code persists after the harness repair
c: Loop G wire shorted to the 12 V supply
Loop output stage damaged by an earlier short and stuck on
Moisture bridging pins in a loop G connector

U3529.d: U3529 marks a fault on circuit H, the eighth interlock loop, without a more specific result. Texas Instruments distinguishes one central loop running through all high-voltage parts from individual loops inside each subsystem that confirm its own assembly.
s: One HV branch or pack unavailable, or no ready mode
Warning about the high-voltage system
c: Connector or disconnect on loop H open
Loop H wiring damaged on chassis or between packs
Code logged by a controller with faulty software rather than a real loop H fault

U352A.d: U352A says the eighth loop is closed but its electrical values leave the calibrated band. In CATL's interlock patent the decision thresholds follow from the loop current, a sensing resistor and the impedance of every HV part in the chain.
s: Fault appears after a repair or conversion
High-voltage system switches off occasionally
c: Replacement HV component with different interlock resistance fitted
Extra connector or harness extension added to loop H
Rising contact resistance at several loop H terminals

U352B.d: U352B reports too low a level on interlock loop H. Apart from a pulled plug or a grounded wire, a deliberate opening can cause it: Texas Instruments mentions feeding a crash signal into the loop so that high voltage shuts off after an accident.
s: High voltage off after an accident or airbag deployment
Vehicle cannot be made ready
c: Loop H opened on purpose by a crash signal after an accident
Loop H wiring or plug damaged in a collision
Loop H wire shorted to ground

U352C.d: U352C reports an excessive reading on loop H. Whether that points to foreign voltage or to a break depends on the quantity the controller evaluates.
s: No ready mode, high-voltage warning
Fault sometimes disappears after moving connectors
c: Loop H wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Corroded or loose terminal raising loop H resistance
Loop source stuck on in the controller

U352D.d: U352D is the summary code for interlock circuit J, the ninth loop in J2012 lettering, which leaves out the letter I. What the loop contains is up to the maker, and none has published it.
s: No ready mode, often right after a hood, trunk or underbody panel was opened
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
Charging blocked
c: Connector in loop J not fully latched
Hood, trunk or access panel latch wired into loop J not fully engaged
Controller that drives and reads loop J faulty

U352E.d: U352E reports an implausible result from loop J. Interlocks also guard auxiliary drives outside the traction system.
s: High-voltage consumer on loop J switching off intermittently
Fault more frequent on rough roads or after work on covers
High-voltage system warning that comes and goes
c: Cover with interlock sensing seated unevenly or gasket deformed
Loose contact in a loop J connector
Sensing element or its actuating magnet loose or damaged
Signal input of the evaluating controller faulty

U352F.d: U352F means loop J reads below its lower threshold, the picture an interrupted loop gives. In high-voltage plugs the interlock pins are shorter than the power pins, so they part first when the plug is withdrawn.
s: High-voltage system switches off and stays off
No ready mode after work near high-voltage plugs
Charging not possible
c: High-voltage plug in loop J partly withdrawn, interlock pins already apart
Interlock pin in loop J pushed back in its cavity
Loop J wire chafed through to ground

U3530.d: U3530 flags loop J above its upper threshold. Foreign voltage is one explanation, but in a design that pushes a constant current through the loop and reads the drop across it, any added resistance lifts the measured value too.
s: Fault appears after long drives or charging, not on a cold start
Charging session or drive interrupted by a high-voltage warning
Loop measures normal once the components have cooled down
c: Cracked solder joint or crimp in loop J whose resistance rises when warm
Loop J wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Loose or spread terminal in a loop J connector

U3531.d: U3531 stands for an unspecified fault on interlock circuit K, the tenth loop. An interlock need not be a dedicated wire pair.
s: No ready mode or one high-voltage branch unavailable
Network or communication codes stored alongside
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
c: Connector in loop K not fully latched
Communication line routed with loop K interrupted or disturbed

U3532.d: U3532 indicates that loop K does not respond the way the controller expects. Some checks run only while the system powers up.
s: Vehicle sometimes does not become ready at switch-on, then works on the next attempt
Fault stored at start-up rather than while driving
c: Marginal contact in a loop K connector that passes some start checks and fails others
Fault in the precharge path disturbing the start-up check
Controller software with outdated check limits

U3533.d: U3533 says loop K reads too low. Apart from an open plug, part of the loop current may be escaping somewhere.
s: Vehicle does not reach ready mode
Fault may follow work on seats or interior trim
Warning to have the high-voltage system checked
c: Loop K wire squeezed against ground by seat, trim or mounting parts
Plug within loop K not connected
High-voltage component on loop K leaking loop current to ground internally

U3534.d: U3534 reports loop K above its upper threshold. Besides a loop wire chafed onto a 12 V feed, the timing of the electronics can be behind it.
s: Vehicle does not become ready
Fault may appear right at switch-on although no wiring damage is found
c: Loop K wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Loop source still disabled when the controller evaluates loop K
Controller software with faulty start-up sequence

U3535.d: U3535 is the umbrella code for interlock circuit L, the eleventh loop. Large vehicles carry many guarded compartments.
s: Vehicle or one energy storage unit unavailable after maintenance
High-voltage system warning on the dashboard
Fault linked to opening or closing a compartment
c: Door or lid limit switch on loop L misadjusted or not actuated
Manual high-voltage interlock or lockout switch left off after service
Connector in loop L not fully latched

U3536.d: U3536 means loop L delivers values the controller considers implausible without a clear limit being crossed. Shaky contacts are a typical reason.
s: Short high-voltage dropouts while driving, especially over bumps
Warning disappears after a restart
c: Terminal in a loop L connector with too little contact force
Loop L connector without proper strain relief, moving with vibration
Signal input of the evaluating controller faulty

U3537.d: U3537 is logged for an insufficient reading on loop L. The cause may lie outside the loop itself.
s: Vehicle or one high-voltage bus does not become ready
Interlock codes for more than one loop stored at once
c: Plug within loop L disconnected or wire shorted to ground
Source of a coupled loop not running, so the coupling relay stays open
Coupling relay between loops with failed coil or contact

U3538.d: U3538 is stored when loop L overshoots its permitted maximum. In a constant-current loop that can be a contact problem rather than foreign voltage.
s: Vehicle does not become ready or switches off high voltage
Heating or air conditioning affected if their plugs are part of the loop
c: Connector revision in loop L with interlock pins too short for reliable contact
Loop L wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Spread female terminal in a loop L connector

U3539.d: U3539 covers a non-specific fault on circuit M, the twelfth interlock loop. Loops J to M only make sense in very extensive high-voltage systems such as trucks, buses, construction or mining machines with interfaces for battery, charging, drive and auxiliaries such as hydraulic pumps or heaters.
s: Vehicle or a high-voltage auxiliary unavailable
High-voltage warning without visible damage
c: Connector of an auxiliary or charging interface in loop M not fully latched
Loop M wiring damaged on a long run through the vehicle

U353A.d: U353A flags loop M as questionable rather than plainly open or shorted. Redundant monitoring can produce exactly that state.
s: Warning lamp while the vehicle keeps driving
Occasional loss of high voltage if the second channel also degrades
c: One of the loop M signal sources weak or failed
Loose contact in a loop M connector distorting the signal
Detection circuit for loop M faulty

U353B.d: U353B is set when loop M reads too low. A lever-type plug can leave it in exactly that state on purpose.
s: No ready mode after service on high-voltage plugs
Fault persists after clearing
c: Lever-type connector in loop M left at its intermediate position
Loop M wire shorted to ground
Loop M source in the controller failed

U353C.d: U353C indicates that loop M exceeds its upper threshold. A loop built from known resistances can be checked point by point.
s: Vehicle does not become ready
High-voltage warning returns after clearing
c: Corroded or loose contact adding resistance in one section of loop M
Loop M wire in contact with a 12 V supply
High-voltage component with internal loop resistance out of specification

U353D.d: U353D is the general code for interlock circuit N, the thirteenth loop in J2012 lettering; designs with that many loops are only conceivable on very large high-voltage systems. No maker documents U353D publicly.
s: No ready mode or no start, often after rain, washing or wading
Isolation fault stored alongside the interlock code
Hybrid or high-voltage system warning in the cluster
c: Water in a loop N connector because a seal is pinched or damaged
Connector in loop N not fully seated
Interlock pins corroded after earlier moisture
Controller that drives and reads loop N faulty

U353E.d: U353E marks loop N as implausible. Such a verdict can stem from electrical interference rather than from the loop wiring.
s: High-voltage warning that appears briefly, sometimes when braking
No fault found on loop resistance checks
Occasional refusal to become ready
c: Interference from another load coupling into the supply of the monitoring controller
Loose contact in a loop N connector
Ferrite or shielding missing after harness repair
Evaluation software of the controller too sensitive

U353F.d: U353F covers a loop N value under the permitted minimum. The defect can sit inside a consumer rather than in the harness.
s: High voltage switches off and stays off
Interlock fault returns although all cable plugs test fine
Auxiliary drive such as the air compressor not running
c: Interlock path inside an HV consumer such as an electric air compressor open or high-resistance
HV cable plug on loop N not reconnected properly
Loop N wire shorted to ground

U3540.d: U3540 reports loop N on the high side of its permitted window. In converted or repowered vehicles the installer often assembles the loop.
s: No ready mode right after a conversion or component swap
High-voltage system warning
Charging blocked
c: Extra contacts, splices or adapter harnesses from a conversion raise loop N resistance
Loop N wire shorted to a 12 V or 24 V feed
Poorly crimped or loose interlock terminal

U3541.d: U3541 denotes trouble on interlock circuit O, the fourteenth loop. What happens next may depend on the operating state.
s: Warning while driving without loss of drive
No ready mode after the vehicle was switched off
Charging refused
c: Connector in loop O not fully latched
Internal fault in an HV component on loop O

U3542.d: U3542 marks loop O as implausible. Interlock trouble often clusters around charging.
s: Vehicle will not start and reports a plugged-in charging cable
Charging does not start or stops
Fault at the beginning or end of a charging session
c: Loose low-voltage contact at the on-board charger carrying loop O
Contact that opens only when components are hot or cold
Internal fault in the on-board charger

U3543.d: With U3543, loop O has dropped under its minimum. Some plug designs let the fitter see the reason.
s: High voltage stays off after work on HV plugs
No ready mode
Charging not possible
c: Rotary HV plug on loop O not turned to its end position
Interlock tab or socket in a loop O plug bent or pushed back
Loop O wire shorted to ground

U3544.d: U3544 sets when loop O delivers too high a value. A plug can hold its specified torque and still sit crooked.
s: Check engine light and hybrid system message right after an HV repair
No ready mode
c: HV plug on loop O torqued down while tilted
Interlock terminals spread by a crooked fitting
Loop O wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Connector bolt thread stripped so the plug cannot be clamped

U3545.d: U3545 is the general fault code for interlock circuit P, the fifteenth loop. Interlock electronics can be harmed by events elsewhere in the drive.
s: Vehicle cannot be made ready
Other drive faults stored at the same time, such as motor or isolation faults
c: Interlock circuit board inside the inverter damaged, e.g. after a motor winding short
Connector in loop P not fully latched
Electrostatic damage to monitoring electronics during service

U3546.d: U3546 marks loop P as implausible. On large vehicles the mechanical routing of HV cables affects the interlock too.
s: Interlock fault that comes and goes, more often on rough roads
High-voltage warning lamp lighting briefly
Brief loss of high-voltage power
c: HV cable without adequate brackets pulling on a loop P plug
Loose contact in a loop P connector
Cable clamp or bracket not refitted after repair

U3547.d: U3547 reports a low value on loop P, and the contactors drop out with it. A design flaw can be the cause too.
s: Sudden loss of propulsion while driving
Contactors open without prior warning
No restart until the loop reads normal
c: Interlock circuit layout covered by a recall, overlay harness not yet fitted
Plug in loop P open or interlock pin pushed back
Loop P wire shorted to ground

U3548.d: U3548 is the high-side code of loop P. When each unit adds a known share of loop resistance, a single suspect can be isolated by substitution.
s: Contactors stay open, no ready mode
High-voltage system warning
Charging blocked
c: Internal interlock section of an HV component too resistive
Loop P wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Loose or poorly crimped interlock terminal in loop P

U3549.d: U3549 covers the electrical circuit of the high-pressure sensor that reads hydrogen pressure on the storage side, upstream of the regulator, where a full system holds up to 70 MPa, the ceiling set by FMVSS 308. Its value feeds the fuel gauge, fill logic and leak checks: a Hyundai patent watches it while the parked car briefly wakes, a GM patent trims it against the more precise low-pressure sensor whenever the regula
s: Hydrogen system warning in the instrument cluster
Fuel gauge or range display missing or implausible
Fuel cell power limited
c: Corroded or damaged connector or wiring between sensor and storage controller
Sensor supply voltage or ground missing

U354A.d: U354A reports an electrical fault on the first temperature sensor of hydrogen tank A. Tank sensors matter most while refuelling: compression heats the gas, and FMVSS 308 slows the pressure ramp once the gas inside passes 85 °C; on the Mirai the tank temperature is passed to the dispenser by infrared.
s: Code sets while refuelling
Hydrogen system warning
Refuelling slower or ends before the tank is full
c: Outdated software in the unit that evaluates the tank sensors
Temperature sensor inside the tank failed (often only as tank assembly)
Open or short in the sensor wiring or connector at the tank

U354B.d: U354B is the circuit code for the second temperature sensor in tank A. One probe cannot capture a long tank during a fast fill: in tests published in the HySafe journal, sensors in on-tank valves at both ends of a Type IV tank finished a fill around 30 °C apart, and the authors concluded that even two positions miss the hottest zone.
s: Tank cannot be filled completely
Hydrogen system warning
c: Wiring or connector fault at the far tank end
Second temperature sensor of tank A failed
Evaluation software misjudging the sensor pair

U354C.d: U354C flags the circuit of the first temperature sensor in tank B. The maker decides which tank is B, and every series fuel cell car has at least two: the first Mirai carried tanks of 60.0 and 62.4 litres, the Clarity a main and a sub tank.
s: Hydrogen system warning
Refuelling limited or interrupted
c: Open or short in the wiring to tank B
Temperature sensor 1 of tank B failed
Input stage of the storage control unit faulty

U354D.d: U354D marks an electrical fault on the second temperature sensor of tank B. Apart from fill control, tank temperature is needed to convert pressure into fuel quantity, because cold gas at a given pressure holds more hydrogen than warm gas.
s: Hydrogen system warning
Fuel gauge less accurate
Refuelling ends early
c: Moisture or damage at the underbody connector of tank B
Temperature sensor 2 of tank B failed
Harness chafed after underbody or tank work

U354E.d: U354E points to an electrical fault on sensor 1 of tank C, a tank that exists only on three-tank vehicles: the second-generation Mirai, whose long central tank is joined by two smaller ones crosswise under the rear seat and the boot, or the Nexo with three tanks holding 156 litres. On a two-tank car such as the first Mirai or the Clarity the code would suggest a configuration or software mismatch.
s: Hydrogen system warning
Refuelling slower or stopped early
c: Wiring or connector fault at tank C
Temperature sensor 1 of tank C failed
Controller coded for a different number of tanks

U354F.d: U354F is set when the circuit of the second temperature sensor in tank C fails. During refuelling the car hands tank data to the station; Toyota describes infrared links between the tank temperature sensors, nozzle and dispenser that set the flow so the gas does not overheat.
s: Refuelling takes longer or stops before full
Hydrogen system warning
Reduced range after refuelling
c: Open or short in the wiring of sensor 2 at tank C
Temperature sensor 2 of tank C failed
Evaluation software needing a manufacturer update

U3550.d: U3550 indicates an electrical fault in the control circuit of the solenoid valve on hydrogen tank A. This on-tank valve is the primary closure between tank and fuel system, and FMVSS 308 requires it to default to closed when unpowered.
s: Hydrogen system warning
Reduced range, or no READY if the car depends on this tank
c: Solenoid coil of the tank A valve open or shorted
Wiring or connector fault between controller and valve
Valve driver stage in the storage control unit faulty

U3551.d: U3551 concerns the enable circuit of the valve on tank A: not the switched control line, but the path that permits the valve to be powered at all, typically a relay, fuse or supply-side switch. Designs keep it apart so a crash can cut hydrogen reliably.
s: No READY or fuel cell does not start
Hydrogen system warning
c: Enable or crash cutoff relay faulty
Blown fuse or missing supply in the valve enable path
Open or short in the enable wiring to valve A

U3552.d: U3552 is the performance code for the valve on tank A: the circuit tests good, but the valve does not act as commanded, either staying shut or failing to seal. With several tanks this is hard to see, because one pressure sensor where the tank lines merge cannot tell that a single tank no longer delivers.
s: Noticeably lower range than the gauge suggests
Hydrogen system warning
c: Tank A valve stuck closed or opening sluggishly
Implausible tank pressure reading misleading the check

U3553.d: U3553 means the controller sees a fault in the drive circuit of the solenoid valve on tank B, such as an open coil, a short to ground or supply, or an output that does not follow its command. Hyundai shows in a patent how such valves can be checked: one current sensor reads the operating current of several tank solenoids; if it falls below a reference, the controller switches the PWM duty from 100 to 90 % and looks w
s: Hydrogen system warning
Range reduced because tank B is not used
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector to the tank B valve
Output stage of the control unit faulty

U3554.d: U3554 refers to the enable path that powers the tank B solenoid. Its purpose is a second, independent way to withdraw the permission for the valve to open.
s: Hydrogen system warning
Range reduced or no READY
c: Enable relay or switch in the supply path faulty
Open or short in the enable line to valve B
Faulty input that withdraws the release, such as a crash or flap signal

U3555.d: U3555 reports that the valve on tank B does not behave as expected although its circuit tests good. Leakage through the closed valve is one form.
s: Hydrogen system warning, sometimes after parking
Range lower than expected
c: Tank B valve seat leaking when closed
Manual tank valve not reopened after service

U3556.d: U3556 is the control circuit code for the valve on tank C, the third tank found only on three-tank layouts such as the Nexo or the current Mirai. On the Mirai the two crosswise tanks behind the long central one are the smaller ones, so losing one costs only part of the range.
s: Hydrogen system warning
Range noticeably shorter after a full fill
c: Wiring or connector fault at the tank C valve
Driver stage for valve C faulty

U3557.d: U3557 is stored for a fault in the enable circuit of the tank C valve, the third tank of three-tank vehicles. Permission to open is not tied to driving alone: a Honda patent describes the cutoff valve being open with the ignition off, for example when the stack keeps operating after shutdown, so collision detection stays powered in that state and a cutoff relay can still close the valve.
s: Hydrogen system warning, possibly right after switch-off or at start
Reduced range
c: Cutoff or enable relay for valve C faulty
Fuse or common valve supply interrupted
Enable line to tank C damaged

U3558.d: U3558 is listed only as Hydrogen Tank C Valve, without a fault type, so it serves as the general valve code for tank C on three-tank vehicles. FMVSS 308 shows what such a valve must withstand: tens of thousands of pressure cycles, partly at extreme temperatures, chatter flow, and afterwards no more than 10 NmL of leakage per hour.
s: Hydrogen system warning
Shorter range
c: Tank C valve sticking or not sealing
Electrical fault at the valve without its own circuit code
Tank and valve beyond their service life

U3559.d: U3559 flags a wiring or signal fault on the first pressure sensor of the air supply that feeds the stack, located behind the air filter and ahead of the electric compressor. Its reading is the suction pressure of the compressor: in a Toyota patent the delivery pressure is divided by it to place the operating point on the compressor map and keep clear of the surge line, and Nissan derives the compressor inlet pressure
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, especially under high load or at altitude
Unusual compressor noise
c: Connector or wiring at the air filter housing wet, corroded or damaged
5 V supply or ground of the sensor missing
Fuel cell control unit faulty or needing a software update

U355A.d: U355A concerns the first of two pressure sensors behind the charge air cooler, where compressed and cooled air heads for the humidifier and the stack. This is the pressure the system really regulates: in a Nissan patent a sensor between intercooler and water recovery unit is the feedback for compressor torque and the outlet pressure valve, and the controller caps this pressure so that compressor and humidifier stay b
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Noticeably reduced power
Compressor speed fluctuates or stays high
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 1
Shared 5 V supply or ground faulty (often with other sensor codes)

U355B.d: U355B points to a circuit problem with pressure sensor 2 at the charge air cooler outlet. J2012 lists two at this spot, which points to a pair used for cross-checking; how a maker splits the roles is unpublished, and no public document uses U355B.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Start refused or system shuts down shortly after a cold start
Reduced power while only one pressure sensor is valid
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 2
Condensed water frozen on the sensor (occurs at cold start, may clear when warm)

U355C.d: U355C reports a circuit fault on the temperature sensor behind the charge air cooler. Compression heats the air strongly: Honda gives about 120 °C at the compressor outlet, while the stack works at 80 to 90 °C, so the air is first brought down to roughly 60 to 75 °C.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power limited, especially under sustained high load
Compressor runs at reduced speed
c: Open or short in wiring or connector of the temperature sensor
Sensor ground or reference circuit faulty

U355D.d: U355D covers the first pressure sensor in front of the expander, a turbine in the cathode exhaust that turns leftover pressure from the stack outlet into shaft power for the compressor. Garrett states that its optional turbine expander, developed among others for the compressor of the BMW iX5 Hydrogen, lowers the electricity needed for compression by up to 20 %.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Higher hydrogen consumption because less energy is recovered
Reduced peak power
c: Wiring or connector of sensor 1 at the wet exhaust side corroded, open or shorted
Expander inlet pressure sensor 1 faulty internally

U355E.d: U355E names a circuit fault on pressure sensor 2 at the expander inlet. Conditions there are harsh: cathode exhaust carries the product water of the stack, and Volkswagen notes in a turbine patent that the pressure drop inside the turbine makes water condense even behind a droplet separator, eroding the blades.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Fault appears mainly after cold starts
Reduced power if sensor 1 is affected as well
c: Wiring or connector of sensor 2 corroded by exhaust moisture, open or shorted
Water frozen in the sensor port at cold start
Expander inlet pressure sensor 2 faulty internally

U355F.d: U355F reports a wiring or output stage fault on the actuator of the valve at the cathode outlet, which throttles the air leaving the stack and thereby sets the pressure the air side runs at. GM moves such a valve in closed loop on a pressure reading, in steps or continuously.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Noticeably reduced power
Fuel cell system shuts down or vehicle does not reach READY
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the valve actuator (wet exhaust area)
Valve motor or actuator winding faulty
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty or software outdated

U3560.d: U3560 is set when the signal of the position sensor on the cathode backpressure valve is missing, shorted or outside its electrical range. Outlet valves of this kind are often throttle flaps whose angle is reported back, as a Hydrogenics patent shows for the cathode and purge valves of a stack.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power
Further air path codes stored at the same time
c: Open, short or moisture in the position sensor wiring or connector
Position sensor faulty (often only available with the valve unit)
Sensor 5 V supply or ground missing

U3561.d: U3561 points to a break, a short or an output stage fault in the actuator circuit of the cathode bypass valve. This valve lets part of the compressor delivery skip the stack and flow straight into the exhaust.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, compressor speed fluctuating at low load
Fuel cell system does not start
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the bypass valve
Bypass valve motor or actuator faulty
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty

U3562.d: Unlike U3561, this code concerns how the cathode bypass valve itself behaves: it does not reach or hold the opening the controller asks for, for instance because it sticks. A Toyota patent shows why a valve stuck shut is serious.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power or failed start in frost
Unusual compressor or air noise
c: Valve frozen in place after a cold soak
Valve sticking from deposits or wear
Actuator too weak or gear damaged
Position feedback reading wrong, valve itself fine

U3563.d: U3563 means the position sensor on the cathode bypass valve delivers no usable signal because of a broken wire, a short or a voltage outside its window. Toyota's patent mounts such a valve body position sensor right at the bypass valve, with pressure sensors before and after it; the angle tells the controller how the compressor air is really being split between stack and bypass.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, especially at low load
c: Open, short or moisture in the position sensor wiring or connector
Position sensor in the valve unit faulty
Shared 5 V supply or ground faulty (often with other sensor codes)

U3564.d: U3564 deals with the wiring of pressure sensor 1 on hydrogen supply line A, most likely the medium-pressure section behind the tank regulator; J2012 does not fix the spot. Toyota's patent shows such a layout: a mechanical reducing valve brings tank hydrogen down to roughly 1.1–1.6 MPa, an intermediate pressure sensor watches that section, and the injector then lowers the pressure to about 200–300 kPa for the stack.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power
Fuel cell system may refuse to start
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of pressure sensor 1
Pressure sensor 1 faulty internally (maker may supply a revised part)
5 V supply or ground of the sensor missing
Fuel cell control unit faulty or needing a software update

U3565.d: U3565 signals that the second pressure sensor of hydrogen supply line A has a wiring problem. Two sensors on one line let the controller cross-check them, and Hyundai's Nexo shows how such a pair is handled in service: when hydrogen pressure sensor 1 or 2 (P315200, P315300) set codes, campaign T4E from 2019 had both swapped for a revised part at an outdoor venting spot, followed by an offset reset and a leak test; th
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Often no noticeable change while sensor 1 still works
Reduced power
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of pressure sensor 2
Sensor membrane damaged during a previous repair
Fuel cell control unit faulty or needing a software update

U3566.d: U3566 is set for an electrical fault at anode inlet pressure sensor 1, sitting between hydrogen injector and stack. A GM patent explains why this value is central: it closes the loop for the injector and also feeds anode valve control and the handling of hydrogen in the exhaust.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Noticeably reduced power
Rough or interrupted fuel cell start
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 1 at the stack
Anode inlet pressure sensor 1 faulty internally
Shared 5 V supply or ground faulty (often with other sensor codes)

U3567.d: U3567 belongs to the second pressure sensor at the anode inlet. Its signal carries safety weight: GM uses anode pressure to catch an injector stuck open, then shuts the tank valves, opens the anode bleed valve, lifts cathode pressure with compressor and backpressure valve and opens the cathode bypass so hydrogen in the exhaust stays diluted.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Often no noticeable change while sensor 1 still works
Reduced power
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 2 at the stack
Anode inlet pressure sensor 2 faulty internally
Water in the connector, fault mainly after frost

U3568.d: U3568 flags trouble in the electrical drive of the anode multifunction valve: an open wire, a short against ground or battery voltage, or a failed output stage. The code title does not say which duties the valve combines; known designs merge draining water and purging nitrogen in one solenoid below the anode water separator.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power dropping off the longer the drive lasts
Fuel cell system shuts down or does not start
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the valve (wet area below the stack)
Solenoid coil of the valve open or shorted
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty

U3569.d: With U3569 the multifunction valve can be driven but does not do what it is told: it stays shut, leaks or reacts too slowly. A solenoid of this kind usually lacks position feedback, so its state is inferred.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, uneven fuel cell output
Start refused or shutdown, mainly after frost
Higher hydrogen consumption
c: Valve frozen shut after parking in frost
Valve sticking or leaking from deposits or worn seat
Water level sensor of the separator reads wrong, valve itself fine

U356A.d: U356A concerns the electrical drive of the solenoid sitting under the anode water trap, which lets condensate leave the hydrogen loop. Hyundai opens it when a level sensor reports a full trap and closes it at a low mark so no hydrogen follows; if that sensor fails, the valve is closed as soon as anode pressure falls faster than a set rate.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power after some driving time
Fuel cell system shuts down
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the drain valve
Drain valve solenoid coil open or shorted
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty

U356B.d: U356B is about how the drain valve behaves, not its wiring. Hyundai shows how such faults are separated: if the level in the trap fails to drop within a set time after an open command while the position sensor still reports closed, the valve is judged stuck shut; the system then limits current, drains on a schedule derived from accumulated charge and runs the stack warmer so water leaves as vapour.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power limited, fuel cell running hotter than usual
System shutdown if the valve stays open
c: Drain valve frozen after parking in frost
Valve sticking or not sealing due to deposits or a worn seat
Water level sensor of the trap faulty, valve itself fine
Drain line downstream of the valve blocked or iced

U356C.d: U356C covers the drive circuit of a second drain valve mounted directly on the anode exhaust header, the channel inside the stack that gathers the gas leaving every cell. GM lists three valves behind the stack: a bleed valve at the top of the anode sump, a drain valve at its bottom and this header valve, which empties into the cathode exhaust.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power limited, especially after parking on a slope
Often no noticeable effect at first
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the header drain valve
Valve solenoid coil open or shorted
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty

U356D.d: U356D is set when the header drain valve responds electrically yet does not empty the header as intended. GM splits each opening into two phases: first water runs out of the header, then nitrogen-rich gas is bled off.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, uneven cell voltages
Higher hydrogen consumption if the valve stays open
c: Header drain valve or its line frozen
Valve sticking or leaking from deposits or a worn seat
Header drain line to the cathode exhaust blocked

U356E.d: U356E refers to the relay that powers the heater on the anode drain valve, more precisely to its coil drive from the fuel cell controller. Drain valves sit in the wettest corner of the hydrogen loop and can freeze shut after a cold night.
s: Fuel cell warning message
Delayed or failed start in frost
Often no noticeable effect in warm weather
c: Open, short or corrosion in the relay coil wiring or connector
Fuse or supply of the relay circuit missing
Relay driver in the fuel cell control unit faulty

U356F.d: U356F reports that the relay feeding the heater on the anode header drain valve cannot be driven properly because its coil circuit is open or shorted. That valve hangs on the stack's anode outlet header, where condensate gathers and can freeze during a cold soak.
s: Fuel cell warning message
Start problems after a frosty night
Battery discharged if the heater stays on
c: Open, short or corrosion in the relay coil wiring or connector
Relay driver in the fuel cell control unit faulty

U3570.d: U3570 signals that the sensor for coolant entering the stack sends a broken, shorted or out-of-range reading. Thermal control is steered by this value: Hyundai describes a three-port valve which gets the stack inlet temperature from the fuel cell control unit over CAN and sets its opening from it, and in a Nissan patent the current drawn from the stack is capped once inlet coolant passes a set point, so that the outl
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, especially under high load
Implausible stack inlet temperature in live data
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the inlet sensor
Inlet coolant temperature sensor faulty internally (drift, internal open)
Coolant seeping past the sensor seal into the connector
Input stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty

U3571.d: U3571 concerns the wiring and signal of sensor 1 in the coolant stream leaving the stack. Coolant is hottest here, so the reading serves as the main overheat guard: GM holds stack outlet temperature mainly with a three-port valve sending coolant past or through the radiator and shuts the stack off when coolant at this point gets too hot.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power reduced or fuel cell system switched off as a precaution
Outlet temperatures of sensor 1 and sensor 2 disagree in live data
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of outlet sensor 1
Outlet temperature sensor 1 faulty internally or drifting
Connector or wiring near the hot outlet line damaged by heat

U3572.d: U3572 is logged when the second coolant temperature sensor at the stack outlet has a wiring or signal problem. No maker explains in public why two sensors share this spot; mutual checking is the obvious reason.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Little or no change in driving as long as sensor 1 is valid
Reduced power if both outlet sensors are affected
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of outlet sensor 2
Shared sensor ground faulty (often with U3571 at the same time)

U3573.d: U3573 concerns how the coolant mixing valve is powered: its actuator line may be interrupted or shorted, or the output stage may have failed. This three-way valve splits stack coolant between radiator and bypass and so decides how warm it is when it returns to the stack.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Stack temperature too high or too low, reduced power
Slow warm-up of the fuel cell system
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the valve actuator
Actuator motor or solenoid coil of the mixing valve faulty
Driver stage or CAN link of the controlling unit faulty

U3574.d: U3574 serves as the catch-all for the coolant mixing valve when the trouble lies in its behaviour rather than its wiring: it sticks, moves too slowly or misses the commanded split between radiator and bypass. Temperatures reveal it, because GM sets stack outlet temperature with this valve and the inlet-to-outlet difference with pump speed, so a jammed valve upsets both.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Stack temperature swings or stays too high under load
Reduced power, slow warm-up in cold weather
c: Valve element sticking from deposits, worn seal or unsuitable coolant
Actuator gear or motor worn, valve moves sluggishly
Internal leak, coolant passes the closed port
Air in the stack coolant loop after service distorting the temperature response

U3575.d: U3575 deals with wiring and signal of the sensor reporting how far the coolant mixing valve is open. GM lists feedback of the valve position, next to two temperature sensors, among the parts its stack outlet temperature control relies on.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Stack temperature regulated less precisely, reduced power
Valve opening shown as invalid in live data
c: Open, short or moisture in the position sensor wiring or connector
Position sensor faulty (usually replaced together with the valve)

U3576.d: U3576 is set when the stack differential pressure sensor delivers no signal, a shorted one or one outside its valid range. The title leaves open which two pressures it compares.
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power or fuel cell system shuts down
No start, especially after a cold night
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the differential pressure sensor
Water or ice in the sensor ports or a failed sensor heater
